claim: The naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) has a reported maximum lifespan of >30 years.
source: The longest-lived rodent, the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber), has a reported maximum lifespan of >30 years and exhibits delayed and/or attenuated age-associated physiological declines.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the data presented in the manuscript showing survival beyond 30 years.

claim: Naked mole-rats exhibit delayed and/or attenuated age-associated physiological declines.
source: The longest-lived rodent, the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber), has a reported maximum lifespan of >30 years and exhibits delayed and/or attenuated age-associated physiological declines.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: The age-specific hazard of mortality in naked mole-rats did not increase with age, regardless of sex or breeding-status.
source: Moreover, unlike all other mammals studied to date, and regardless of sex or breeding-status, the age-specific hazard of mortality did not increase with age, even at ages 25-fold past their time to reproductive maturity.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by Kaplan-Meier analyses and hazard calculations shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Naked mole-rats do not show increased hazard of mortality even at ages 25-fold past their time to reproductive maturity.
source: Moreover, unlike all other mammals studied to date, and regardless of sex or breeding-status, the age-specific hazard of mortality did not increase with age, even at ages 25-fold past their time to reproductive maturity.
evidence: This is calculated from the data showing constant hazard from 6 months (Tsex) to beyond 12 years of age.

claim: The absence of hazard increase with age in naked mole-rats defies Gompertz's law.
source: This absence of hazard increase with age, in defiance of Gompertz's law, uniquely identifies the naked mole-rat as a non-aging mammal, confirming its status as an exceptional model for biogerontology.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of established mortality theory (Gompertz's law).

claim: The naked mole-rat is a non-aging mammal.
source: This absence of hazard increase with age, in defiance of Gompertz's law, uniquely identifies the naked mole-rat as a non-aging mammal, confirming its status as an exceptional model for biogerontology.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the lack of increasing mortality hazard with age.

claim: The naked mole-rat is recognized as an animal model of biogerontological interest.
source: The longest-lived rodent, the naked mole-rat (Ctenohystrica, Heterocephalus glaber) is recognized as an animal model of biogerontological interest (Buffenstein, 2005; Austad, 2010; Edrey et al., 2011; de Magalhães et al., 2007a) with a maximal lifespan of more than 30 years in our captive care (Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The naked mole-rat has a maximal lifespan of more than 30 years in captive care.
source: The longest-lived rodent, the naked mole-rat (Ctenohystrica, Heterocephalus glaber) is recognized as an animal model of biogerontological interest (Buffenstein, 2005; Austad, 2010; Edrey et al., 2011; de Magalhães et al., 2007a) with a maximal lifespan of more than 30 years in our captive care (Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation and the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The naked mole-rat's maximum lifespan is five-fold greater than predicted allometrically for a 40 g rodent.
source: This maximum lifespan is five-fold greater than predicted allometrically for a 40 g rodent (Edrey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work that established this comparison.

claim: In the wild, breeding female naked mole-rats remain in the same colony for 17 years.
source: Even in the wild, naked mole-rats are also considered to be very long-lived rodents with reports of breeding females remaining 17 years in the same colony while non-breeders remain 2–3 years (Hochberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hochberg et al., 2016.

claim: In the wild, non-breeding naked mole-rats remain in colonies for 2-3 years.
source: Even in the wild, naked mole-rats are also considered to be very long-lived rodents with reports of breeding females remaining 17 years in the same colony while non-breeders remain 2–3 years (Hochberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hochberg et al., 2016.

claim: Most wild rodents live only a season in the wild.
source: In sharp contrast, other rodents generally last only a season in the wild, with their young-age deaths attributed to predation, inclement weather, parasites, pathogens and lack of food resources (Morgen, 2003; David and Jarvis, 1985; Boonstra and Krebs, 2012; Krebs et al., 1995; Krebs et al., 1973).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Young-age deaths in wild rodents are attributed to predation, inclement weather, parasites, pathogens and lack of food resources.
source: In sharp contrast, other rodents generally last only a season in the wild, with their young-age deaths attributed to predation, inclement weather, parasites, pathogens and lack of food resources (Morgen, 2003; David and Jarvis, 1985; Boonstra and Krebs, 2012; Krebs et al., 1995; Krebs et al., 1973).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Laboratory mice live almost an order of magnitude longer than their wild counterparts.
source: Laboratory mice, cosseted in a protected environment with ad libitum resources, live almost an order of magnitude longer than their wild counterparts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about laboratory versus wild mouse lifespans.

claim: Laboratory mice live only half as long as expected on the basis of body size.
source: Nevertheless, these small mammals live only half as long as expected on the basis on body size and lifespan is limited by age-related, exponentially increasing intrinsic risk of dying (Miller et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Miller et al., 2002.

claim: Laboratory mouse lifespan is limited by age-related, exponentially increasing intrinsic risk of dying.
source: Nevertheless, these small mammals live only half as long as expected on the basis on body size and lifespan is limited by age-related, exponentially increasing intrinsic risk of dying (Miller et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Miller et al., 2002.

claim: The difference between captive and wild longevity records for naked mole-rats likely reflects a lower incidence of extrinsic rather than intrinsic mortality in captivity.
source: Similarly, the difference between captive and wild longevity records for naked mole-rats likely reflects a lower incidence of extrinsic rather than intrinsic mortality in captivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between wild and captive lifespans.

claim: What determines naked mole-rat lifespans in captivity is currently unknown.
source: What determines naked mole-rat lifespans in captivity is currently unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The naked mole-rat is a strictly subterranean, mouse-sized rodent.
source: The naked mole-rat is a strictly subterranean, mouse-sized rodent and is one of only two known eusocial mammals; it lives in large family groups (colonies) of up to 300 individuals (average colony size = 60).
evidence: This is a direct description of the species.

claim: The naked mole-rat is one of only two known eusocial mammals.
source: The naked mole-rat is a strictly subterranean, mouse-sized rodent and is one of only two known eusocial mammals; it lives in large family groups (colonies) of up to 300 individuals (average colony size = 60).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Naked mole-rats live in large family groups (colonies) of up to 300 individuals with an average colony size of 60.
source: The naked mole-rat is a strictly subterranean, mouse-sized rodent and is one of only two known eusocial mammals; it lives in large family groups (colonies) of up to 300 individuals (average colony size = 60).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species' social structure.

claim: The underground lifestyle of naked mole-rats in arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa poses numerous ecological and physiological challenges.
source: Their underground lifestyle in the arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa poses numerous ecological and physiological challenges, such as difficulty locating food underground, impaired heat and gas exchange, low oxygen availability, and exposure to heavy metals and other chemicals in soil and plant-defense toxins (Buffenstein, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Buffenstein, 2000.

claim: The underground lifestyle of naked mole-rats protects against dangers such as predation and above-ground climate extremes.
source: But this milieu also protects against dangers such as predation and above-ground climate extremes (e.g., cold, wind and rain), thereby providing several survival advantages (Buffenstein, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Buffenstein, 2005.

claim: Breeding in each naked mole-rat colony is monopolized by only one female (the 'queen') and 1 to 3 males at a time.
source: Breeding in each colony is monopolized by only one female (the 'queen') and 1 to 3 males at a time, with most animals in the colony showing no sexual behaviors throughout their life, but rather helping with the overall maintenance and survival of the colony, including care of pups (Jarvis, 1981).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Jarvis, 1981.

claim: Most naked mole-rats in a colony show no sexual behaviors throughout their life.
source: Breeding in each colony is monopolized by only one female (the 'queen') and 1 to 3 males at a time, with most animals in the colony showing no sexual behaviors throughout their life, but rather helping with the overall maintenance and survival of the colony, including care of pups (Jarvis, 1981).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Jarvis, 1981.

claim: Queen status in naked mole-rat colonies is primarily maintained through physical intimidation of subordinates.
source: Queen status is primarily maintained through physical intimidation of subordinates and should the queen die or a non-reproductive subordinate be removed from the colony, subordinates can become reproductively active (Clarke and Faulkes, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Clarke and Faulkes, 1997.

claim: If the queen dies or a non-reproductive subordinate is removed from the colony, subordinates can become reproductively active.
source: Queen status is primarily maintained through physical intimidation of subordinates and should the queen die or a non-reproductive subordinate be removed from the colony, subordinates can become reproductively active (Clarke and Faulkes, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Clarke and Faulkes, 1997.

claim: Attainment of breeder-status for either sex is accompanied by morphological, physiological and behavioral changes.
source: Attainment of breeder-status for either sex, regardless of age, is accompanied by morphological, physiological and behavioral changes, including changes in body size, brain volume and reproductive organ morphology (O'Riain et al., 2000; Holmes et al., 2007; Peroulakis et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Across vertebrates, adult body mass is a strong correlate of longevity, with larger species living longer than smaller species.
source: Across vertebrates, adult body mass is a strong correlate, with larger species living longer than smaller species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Naked mole-rats live almost five-fold longer than expected based on their body mass.
source: Naked mole-rats live exceptionally long vis-à-vis this metric: almost five-fold longer than expected (Hulbert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hulbert et al., 2007.

claim: Species' ages of reproductive maturity (Tsex) are predictive of their lifespans.
source: Species' ages of reproductive maturity (Tsex) are also predictive of their lifespans (Hamilton, 1966; Rose et al., 2007; Prothero, 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Naked mole-rats have a gestation length of 66-76 days.
source: Relative to Tsex, naked mole-rats are once again long-lived outliers: despite a long gestation length (66–76 days) and a six-month elapse from birth to reproductive capacity (Edrey et al., 2011), they live over three-fold longer than expected by this metric (de Magalhães et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Edrey et al., 2011.

claim: Naked mole-rats reach reproductive capacity six months from birth.
source: Relative to Tsex, naked mole-rats are once again long-lived outliers: despite a long gestation length (66–76 days) and a six-month elapse from birth to reproductive capacity (Edrey et al., 2011), they live over three-fold longer than expected by this metric (de Magalhães et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Edrey et al., 2011.

claim: Naked mole-rats live over three-fold longer than expected based on their age of reproductive maturity.
source: Relative to Tsex, naked mole-rats are once again long-lived outliers: despite a long gestation length (66–76 days) and a six-month elapse from birth to reproductive capacity (Edrey et al., 2011), they live over three-fold longer than expected by this metric (de Magalhães et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to de Magalhães et al., 2007b.

claim: Physiological declines that accompany advancing age in most mammals fail to manifest in naked mole-rats.
source: Beyond lifespan, the physiological declines that accompany advancing age in most mammals fail to manifest in naked mole-rats (Buffenstein, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Buffenstein, 2008.

claim: Breeding female naked mole-rats show no menopause and retain high fertility even at ages past 30 years.
source: Breeding females show no menopause, retaining high fertility even at ages past 30 years (Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016.

claim: Neurogenesis in naked mole-rats is prolonged and may continue for at least two decades.
source: Neurogenesis is also prolonged and may continue for at least two decades (Holmes, 2016), and over a similar time course, no significant changes in cardiac function (Grimes et al., 2014), body composition, bone quality, and metabolism (O'Connor et al., 2002) are evident.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Holmes, 2016.

claim: No significant changes in cardiac function occur in naked mole-rats over at least two decades.
source: Neurogenesis is also prolonged and may continue for at least two decades (Holmes, 2016), and over a similar time course, no significant changes in cardiac function (Grimes et al., 2014), body composition, bone quality, and metabolism (O'Connor et al., 2002) are evident.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Grimes et al., 2014.

claim: No significant changes in body composition, bone quality, and metabolism occur in naked mole-rats over at least two decades.
source: Neurogenesis is also prolonged and may continue for at least two decades (Holmes, 2016), and over a similar time course, no significant changes in cardiac function (Grimes et al., 2014), body composition, bone quality, and metabolism (O'Connor et al., 2002) are evident.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to O'Connor et al., 2002.

claim: Age-associated chronic diseases such as cancer are rare in naked mole-rats.
source: Age-associated chronic diseases such as cancer are also rare (Edrey et al., 2011; Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Edrey et al., 2011 and Lewis and Buffenstein, 2016.

claim: Proteasome function is maintained with age in naked mole-rats.
source: Within the cell, proteasome function, as well as mitochondrial mass, gene and protein expression are maintained with age (Pérez et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Pérez et al., 2009 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: Mitochondrial mass, gene and protein expression are maintained with age in naked mole-rats.
source: Within the cell, proteasome function, as well as mitochondrial mass, gene and protein expression are maintained with age (Pérez et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Pérez et al., 2009 and Kim et al., 2011.

claim: Species from safer habitats tend to live longer; those from more dangerous habitats tend to mature rapidly, reproduce early and die young.
source: These molecular and physiological observations reflect broader phylogenic trends with respect to mortality and life history traits: species from safer habitats tend to live longer; those from more dangerous habitats tend to mature rapidly, reproduce early and die young (Ricklefs, 1998; Pianka, 1970).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Ricklefs, 1998 and Pianka, 1970.

claim: The Gompertz-Makeham law of mortality defines age-specific hazard as h(t) = αeβt + γ.
source: The concepts of mortality and physiological decline associated with aging can be connected within the mathematical framework of the Gompertz-Makeham law of mortality (Gavrilov and Gavrilova, 1991). Age-specific hazard h(t) is defined by the equation h(t) = αeβt + γ.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gavrilov and Gavrilova, 1991.

claim: The Gompertzian component of hazard (αeβt) describes hazard that increases exponentially with age due to intrinsic age-related physiological declines.
source: The first term (αeβt) describes the Gompertzian component of hazard, originally derived from examination of human life tables (Gompertz, 1825). This hazard increases exponentially with age, presumably due to intrinsic age-related physiological declines.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gompertz, 1825.

claim: In the Gompertz-Makeham framework, β defines the rate-of-aging with respect to mortality.
source: In this framework, β defines the rate-of-aging with respect to mortality: its value determines the doubling time for mortal hazard (for humans, ~7–8.5 years; [Finch et al., 1990]).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Finch et al., 1990.

claim: For humans, the doubling time for mortal hazard is approximately 7-8.5 years.
source: In this framework, β defines the rate-of-aging with respect to mortality: its value determines the doubling time for mortal hazard (for humans, ~7–8.5 years; [Finch et al., 1990]).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Finch et al., 1990.

claim: The Makeham component (γ) describes a constant, extrinsically-imposed minimum hazard.
source: The second term (γ) describes the Makeham component: a constant, extrinsically-imposed minimum hazard that can obfuscate Gompertzian hazard at younger ages (Makeham, 1860).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Makeham, 1860.

claim: The dataset analyzed included over 3000 naked mole-rat lifespan data points.
source: We compiled and analyzed a large compendium of historical naked mole-rat lifespan data with >3000 data points.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: The dataset drew from 3848 historically catalogued naked mole-rats.
source: Our data set drew from 3848 historically catalogued naked mole-rats from our own collection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: 3329 naked mole-rats had high resolution (day/month/year) records of date-of-birth and date-of-death/censorship.
source: Of these, 3329 had high resolution (day/month/year) records of date-of-birth and date-of-death/censorship, allowing them to be included in our initial, most stringent analysis (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: 61.6% of the naked mole-rat population survived across the 30 year timespan covered by the data set.
source: The construction of a Kaplan-Meier survival curve for naked mole-rats starting at their Tsex (183 days) revealed 61.6% of the population to have survived across the 30 year timespan covered by the data set (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The estimated probability of death per day for naked mole-rats never exceeded 1/10,000.
source: Although slightly higher in the months immediately following Tsex (d183-400), hazard remained consistently low thereafter, with the estimated probability of death per day never exceeding 1/10,000.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Low mortality hazard persisted in naked mole-rats for more than two decades.
source: Low hazard persisted for more than two decades, including in the final estimate bin, which was estimated using the final recorded death (including that event, at day 6529) and all subsequent censorship data, and for which mortality hazard was estimated to be 1.8 * 10−5 per day.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mortality hazard for naked mole-rats at day 6529 was estimated to be 1.8 * 10−5 per day.
source: Low hazard persisted for more than two decades, including in the final estimate bin, which was estimated using the final recorded death (including that event, at day 6529) and all subsequent censorship data, and for which mortality hazard was estimated to be 1.8 * 10−5 per day.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The inclusion of less-reliable data did not modify the properties of the overall Kaplan-Meier survival profile.
source: The inclusion of less-reliable data did not modify the properties of the overall Kaplan-Meier survival profile (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a notable survival difference between breeding versus non-breeding status, with breeders enjoying higher survival than non-breeders.
source: There was a notable survival difference between breeding versus non-breeding status, with breeders enjoying higher survival than non-breeders.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Survival did not observably differ between male versus female breeders.
source: However, survival did not observably differ between male versus female breeders.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mortal hazard of breeders was approximately 5-10 fold lower than that of non-breeders.
source: Differential survival made only a minor contribution to this difference: the mortal hazards of breeders was ~5–10 fold lower than that of non-breeders (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In neither breeders nor non-breeders did the mortal hazard increase with age.
source: In neither case did the mortal hazard increase with age; analysis was not carried as far into lifespan as in Figure 1 due to diminished statistical power, but no increase was observable at least until 2000 days of life for both breeding and non-breeding males and females.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Simulations supported the relevance of a non-hazard-increasing mortality model to the full historical data set.
source: Simulations supported the relevance of a non-hazard-increasing mortality model to our full historical data set
evidence: This is the title of a Results subsection and supported by the simulation data in Figure 4.

claim: For laboratory mice, Gompertzian hazard manifests before 800 days-of-life, which is approximately 55% of maximum lifespan.
source: When we plotted the age-specific hazard of laboratory mice (Mus musculus) using the raw data for the control mice cohort from the published paper of Miller (Miller et al., 2014), its exponential (i.e., Gompertzian) nature manifested before 800 days-of-life~55% of maximum lifespan (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For mice, the time from Tsex to median post-Tsex lifespan was 805 days.
source: For mice, the time from Tsex (42 days post-natal; (Tacutu et al., 2013) to median post-Tsex lifespan (847 days) was 805 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Tacutu et al., 2013.

claim: For mice, the time from median lifespan to maximal lifespan (95th percentile) was 294 days.
source: The time from median lifespan to maximal lifespan (defined here as the 95th percentile of post-Tsex lifespans: 1,141 days for mice) was only 294 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: For mice, the latter half of the survival curve was only 37% of the time from median lifespan to maximal lifespan.
source: The latter half of the survival curve was therefore only 37% of the time from median lifespan to maximal lifespan.
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in the Results section.

claim: For human females, post-Tsex median lifespan was 77.8 years.
source: For human females, with Tsex defined as 16 years (mean age-at-menarche of >12.5 years, plus three years to 50% ovulatory-vs-anovulatory cycle frequency (Apter, 1980; Anderson et al., 2003); post-Tsex median lifespan was 77.8 years, and post-Tsex maximal (95th percentile) lifespan was 96.5 years.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Apter, 1980 and Anderson et al., 2003.

claim: For human females, post-Tsex maximal (95th percentile) lifespan was 96.5 years.
source: For human females, with Tsex defined as 16 years (mean age-at-menarche of >12.5 years, plus three years to 50% ovulatory-vs-anovulatory cycle frequency (Apter, 1980; Anderson et al., 2003); post-Tsex median lifespan was 77.8 years, and post-Tsex maximal (95th percentile) lifespan was 96.5 years.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Apter, 1980 and Anderson et al., 2003.

claim: For human females, the median-to-maximal-lifespan time was 30% of the Tsex-to-median-lifespan time.
source: The Tsex-to-median-lifespan time was therefore 61.8 years, and the median-to-maximal-lifespan time was 18.7 years: the latter was 30% of the former.
evidence: This is calculated from the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Naked mole-rats distinguished themselves from other mammals by failing to exhibit an increase in mortality hazard even at ages 25-fold greater than the age of sexual maturity.
source: When compared to these other mammals, naked mole-rats distinguished themselves qualitatively and quantitatively by failing to exhibit an increase in mortality hazard even at ages 25-fold greater than the age of sexual maturity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Aging is typically observable in mammals in the form of an increase in mortality hazard as organisms get older.
source: Aging, defined as the inevitable physiological decline over the lifespan of an organism that weakens homeostasis and increases vulnerability to environmental challenge, is typically observable in mammals in the form of an increase in mortality hazard as organisms get older.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: A decrease in the rise-rate of hazard has been reported in multiple studies involving experimental interventions that extend lifespan and is consistently interpreted as a slowing of aging itself.
source: A decrease in the rise-rate of hazard has been reported in multiple studies involving experimental interventions that extend lifespan (e.g., caloric restriction), and is consistently interpreted as a slowing of aging itself (Fok et al., 2014; Yen and Mobbs, 2008; Simons et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Aging was not observed in the analysis of naked mole-rat mortality, regardless of sex or breeding status.
source: By that metric, 'aging' was not observed at all in our analysis of naked mole-rat mortality, regardless of sex or breeding status.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: The apparent lack-of-aging in naked mole-rats agrees with a large body of literature documenting negligible systems-based senescence in naked mole-rats.
source: This apparent lack-of-aging agrees thematically with a large body of literature documenting negligible systems-based senescence in naked mole-rats (Edrey et al., 2011; Buffenstein, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Edrey et al., 2011 and Buffenstein, 2008.

claim: As mammals get older, even long-lived species conform to Gompertzian laws of mortality.
source: It places this species in a unique demographic position among mammals: as mammals get older, even long-lived species conform to Gompertzian laws of mortality (Jones et al., 2014; Cohen, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Jones et al., 2014 and Cohen, 2017.

claim: The Makeham component describes a background level of extrinsic hazard that obscures Gompertzian intrinsic hazard early in life.
source: The non-increasing hazard could have simply reflected the Makeham component of the Gompertz-Makeham law, a background level of extrinsic hazard that obscures Gompertzian intrinsic hazard early in life.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the Gompertz-Makeham law.

claim: The Makeham component describes human mortality until age approximately 40 years.
source: Such a model describes human mortality until age ~40 years (Bell and Miller, 2005) (Figure 5C) and horse mortality until age ~6 years (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Bell and Miller, 2005 and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Makeham component describes horse mortality until age approximately 6 years.
source: Such a model describes human mortality until age ~40 years (Bell and Miller, 2005) (Figure 5C) and horse mortality until age ~6 years (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The baseline hazard rate for non-breeder naked mole-rats is approximately 1/10,000 per day.
source: However, given the extremely low baseline hazard rate of 1/10,000 per day for non-breeders and ~1/100,000 for breeders, it seems unlikely that the Gompertzian hazard is being overwhelmed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: The baseline hazard rate for breeder naked mole-rats is approximately 1/100,000 per day.
source: However, given the extremely low baseline hazard rate of 1/10,000 per day for non-breeders and ~1/100,000 for breeders, it seems unlikely that the Gompertzian hazard is being overwhelmed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: Under a delayed-aging model, naked mole-rats distinguish themselves from other mammals through an unprecedentedly-long adulthood prior to the emergence of Gompertzian hazard.
source: But even under a delayed-aging model, naked mole-rats profoundly distinguish themselves from other mammals: in this context, through an unprecedentedly-long adulthood prior to the emergence of Gompertzian hazard.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the data.

claim: Naked mole-rat mortality is more consistent with an exponential decay model than with a typical Gompertz model of hazard.
source: Indeed, naked mole-rat mortality was less consistent with a typical Gompertz model of hazard than it was with an exponential decay model, with a constant probability of decay (death) defining a species' half-life.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: For naked mole-rats, the high estimate for per-day hazard of approximately 1/10,000 for non-breeders would correspond to a half-life (median lifespan) of approximately 6900 days (19 years).
source: For naked mole-rats, even the high estimate for per-day hazard of ~1/10,000 that was obtained for non-breeders (Figure 3A) would correspond to a half-life (i.e., median lifespan) of ~6900 days (19 years).
evidence: This is calculated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: Under an exponential decay model, the concept of a 'maximal lifespan' loses relevance because mortality hazard never grows into an insurmountable obstacle.
source: Under an exponential decay model, the concept of a 'maximal lifespan' loses relevance: at no point does mortality hazard grow into an insurmountable obstacle.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the exponential decay model.

claim: Demographic aging is defined by the increase of intrinsic hazard with age.
source: Demographic aging is defined by the increase of intrinsic hazard with age (Gavrilov and Gavrilova, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gavrilov and Gavrilova, 2015.

claim: Analyses of captive naked mole-rats confidently revealed a lack of demographic aging up to at least 4400 days of life (approximately 12 years).
source: Our analyses of captive naked mole-rats confidently revealed a lack of demographic aging up to at least 4400 days of life (~12 years) and strongly suggested no demographic aging far beyond that age (Figure 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Analyses of captive naked mole-rats strongly suggested no demographic aging far beyond 12 years of age.
source: Our analyses of captive naked mole-rats confidently revealed a lack of demographic aging up to at least 4400 days of life (~12 years) and strongly suggested no demographic aging far beyond that age (Figure 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most mammals show signs of demographic aging within a few fold of Tsex.
source: Most mammals live beyond that age, as is required to provide progeny with support and nurturing (Lee, 2003), but show signs of demographic aging within a few fold of Tsex; from this perspective, the naked mole-rat is exceptional, showing no signs of demographic aging many dozens-of-fold beyond Tsex (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lee, 2003 and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The naked mole-rat shows no signs of demographic aging many dozens-of-fold beyond Tsex.
source: Most mammals live beyond that age, as is required to provide progeny with support and nurturing (Lee, 2003), but show signs of demographic aging within a few fold of Tsex; from this perspective, the naked mole-rat is exceptional, showing no signs of demographic aging many dozens-of-fold beyond Tsex (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: A 35-gram rodent would be expected to live up to six years based on body size.
source: Twelve years can also be considered in the context of the expected total lifespan of a naked mole-rat based on its body size (de Magalhães et al., 2007b): this 35-gram rodent would be expected to live up to six years, but instead has not shown the first sign of demographic aging at twice that age.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to de Magalhães et al., 2007b.

claim: The naked mole-rat has not shown the first sign of demographic aging at twice the expected lifespan based on body size.
source: Twelve years can also be considered in the context of the expected total lifespan of a naked mole-rat based on its body size (de Magalhães et al., 2007b): this 35-gram rodent would be expected to live up to six years, but instead has not shown the first sign of demographic aging at twice that age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: Natural lifespan in the wild for naked mole-rats is estimated to be 2-3 years.
source: Twelve years could finally be considered from the perspective of natural lifespan in the wild, which is estimated to be 2–3 years for the naked mole-rat (Hochberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hochberg et al., 2016.

claim: Senescence is difficult to observe in wild rodent populations.
source: Senescence is difficult to observe in wild rodent populations (David and Jarvis, 1985; Krebs et al., 1995; Krebs et al., 1973; Slade, 1995) with most rodents living less than a year (Stueck and Barrett, 1978)
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Most wild rodents live less than a year.
source: Senescence is difficult to observe in wild rodent populations (David and Jarvis, 1985; Krebs et al., 1995; Krebs et al., 1973; Slade, 1995) with most rodents living less than a year (Stueck and Barrett, 1978)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Stueck and Barrett, 1978.

claim: Senescence is easily observed for rats and mice in captivity, not far beyond their typical natural lifespans.
source: Nonetheless, senescence is easily observed for those rodent species (rats and mice) in captivity, not far beyond their typical natural lifespans (Figure 5B; [Gavrilova and Gavrilov, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gavrilova and Gavrilov, 2015 and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For the naked mole-rat, demographic aging is absent 4-to-6-fold beyond their natural lifespans.
source: For the naked mole-rat, demographic aging is absent 4-to-6-fold beyond their natural lifespans.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the data presented.

claim: Naked mole-rats fail to exhibit any evidence for intrinsic hazard contributing to their mortality, even at ages far beyond their expected maximum lifespans.
source: In summary, naked mole-rats fail to exhibit any evidence for intrinsic hazard contributing to their mortality, even at ages far beyond their expected maximum lifespans based on multiple other aspects of their biology or their full lifespans observed in the wild.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Naked mole-rats establish themselves as a non-aging mammal.
source: In doing so, they establish themselves as a non-aging mammal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as the main conclusion.

claim: The progenitors of the naked mole-rats used in this study were collected in Kenya in 1980.
source: The progenitors of the naked mole-rats used in this study were collected by Jennifer Jarvis, Kate Davies, Mike Griffin and Rochelle Buffenstein in Kenya in 1980 and have been housed and cared for at several institutions in South Africa (University of Cape Town and The Medical School of the University of the Witwatersrand) and the USA (City College of New York, University of Texas Health Center at San Antonio and the Buck Institute).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Naked mole-rats were housed in multi-chambered plexiglass burrow systems in rooms maintained at 28-30°C and 30-50% relative humidity.
source: Naked mole-rats were housed in multi-chambered plexiglass burrow systems in rooms maintained at 28–30°C and 30–50% relative humidity, in keeping with climatic conditions in their native habitat.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: At 90 days of age, individual naked mole-rats were sexed, weighed and microchipped.
source: At 90 days of age, individual mole-rats were sexed, weighed and microchipped, using 12 mm Avid MUSICC microchips, and thereby assigned a unique 9-digit identifier.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Kaplan-Meier survival was calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method.
source: For Figures 1–4, survival was calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method (Kaplan and Meier, 1958).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: Confidence intervals were calculated using the Wilson score interval with continuity correction.
source: Confidence intervals were calculated using the Wilson score interval with continuity correction (Newcombe, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.
